narrative:
The model predicted a 62.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was the strongest influence. Although this is higher than the 3.23 average among accepted students, the model determined that it still increased your risk of failing the bar. Your performance in the third year of law school came next; ranking in the 9th decile was actually helpful and pushed the prediction toward passing. Finally, your upper-middle family income also worked against you. While 45% of accepted students come from the same income bracket, the model associated this background with a higher likelihood of bar exam failure in your specific combination of circumstances.

Taken together, these pieces of information led the system to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam, resulting in the denial.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Consider targeted bar exam preparation courses, especially those that build on undergraduate-level reasoning, and look for ways to demonstrate improved performance in later law school milestones. Reapplying with additional evidence of bar readiness could improve your chances in the future. (218 words)
